The Chang is a Persian angular harp, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 322.12. It sounds through its strings, and in ancient times the body was often covered with sheepskin or goatskin, while the strings were of gut or twisted wool and later also nylon; in medieval Azerbaijan eighteen to twenty-four strings were common. It is played by plucking the strings with the fingernails of the right hand or with a plectrum, while the left hand presses the strings for slides, vibrato and ornaments. It was popular in the ancient Persian court and is also found under names in Turkey, Georgia and elsewhere; in ancient times it was played mainly by women, and today it is used in small ensembles, religious ceremonies and parties.
Chang 為波斯豎琴，約公元前4000年見於波斯繪畫與牆面藝術，早期為拱形豎琴: The Chang is a Persian harp, seen in Persian painting and wall art from about 4000 BC; it was an arched harp at first and turned into an angular harp in the early 1900s BC. Between about 300 BC and AD 1 its form changed from a hand-held instrument to a large standing harp, its favour at the Sasanian court made it popular, and in the late period it was made light and easy to carry, becoming the chief harp of Islamic Iran. The name also appears for the Chinese fangxiang and the Uzbek struck dulcimer, it is the origin of the Burmese harp's name, and it was known in the Ottoman Empire too, disappearing from Turkish folk music after the nineteenth century.

It sounds by plucking the strings with the fingernails of the right hand or a thumb plectrum, while the left hand presses the strings to make slides, vibrato and other ornaments, and other plucking techniques are occasionally used as well. Its way of playing differs from that of other Persian instruments: a beginner must first master the division of work between the hands, then practise the pressure of the stopped strings and the ornaments; because the technique is not easy, few people learn it. The instrument is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 322.12, found in Persia, Turkey, Georgia and neighbouring regions.

The treble is bright and crisp and carries well, the middle register warm and full, the bass deep and forceful. Its range is wide, spanning more than three octaves. Its resonance comes mainly from a wooden soundbox, and the timbre varies with the material and tension of the strings. Traditional silk strings sound soft and elegant, modern nylon strings brighter and firmer. Against the inward, desolate guqin, the zheng is more outgoing and brilliant; against the hard, mechanical feel of the piano, it has more human warmth. Its particular slides and stopped notes give it great expressive range, and it can stand on its own or blend with other instruments.
